full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed J: The appellants in these two separate appeals are challenging the order of the High Court Division dismissing their appeals from their conviction and sentence passed by the Special Judge, Comilla, under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958. Two question call for determination in these two appeals by special leave; one, which is purely a question of interpretation of Statutes, is whether the provision for taking cognizance of an offence only on a complaint from a court under section 195 (1) (c) of the Criminal Procedure Code has been dispensed with by the special procedure laid down in the Criminal Law Amendment Act for trial of certain offences; and the other question, if, of course, the first question is answered in the negative, is whether the facts of the instant case in which the impugned conviction has been recorded, bring it within the four comers of section 195 (1) (c) of the Code requiring a complaint from Court for the purpose of taking cognizance of the offence found committed by the appellants. 

 2. Appellant, Muslim Khan, a Mukhtear-cum-Revenue Agent and appellant Sanaullah Akhand, a Member of the public, along with one Syed Ahmed Patwary, a public servant, dead since then, were convicted by the Special Judge on 2 July 1969 under sections 466, 466/109, 471 and 120B of the Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for three years and also to fine of Taka 1000, in default, to rigorous imprisonment for six months more. Against this conviction they preferred two separate appeals, Criminal Appeals Nos. 343 and 349 of 1969, which were dismissed by the High Court Division by the impugned judgment dated 14 August 1984. 

 3. This case arose from an incident of forgery of two documents relating to an auction sale in connection with a Certificate Proceeding. The Certificate Proceeding in question is CC No. 941/1963-64 of the Court of Certificate Officer, Chandpur. One Harekrishna Das was the Certificate debtor in that Certificate case and his land measuring one acre was directed to be sold in auction for realization of some government dues. On 12-3-1964 a public auction was held for the purpose and three brothers namely, Abdul Ghani Akhand, Korban Ali Akhand and Nur Mohammad Akhand purchased it by offering the highest bid. To represent them in the bidding, they had engaged appellant Muslim Khan, Revenue Agent, by executing a Vokalatnama which was also referred to as Agent-nama in the Bid sheet Appellant Muslim Khan accepted the Agent nama and participated in the bid on behalf of the three brothers. The sale was entered in the Sale Register of Certificate Cases showing these three brothers, Abdul Ghani Akhand, Korban Ali Akhand and Mur Mohammad Akhand as the three joint purchasers. The sale was duly confirmed and possession of the land was also delivered to them. The purchasers who reside in a village directed their nephew, appellant Sanaullah Akhand, to obtain the Sale Certificate the writ of possession from the Certificate Officer, but appellant Sanaullah Akhand after some procrastination disclosed that he was one of the three purchasers in the auction, the other two being Abdul Ghani Akhand and Korban Ali Akhand; that is, according to his claim, the third brother Nur Mohammad Akhand was not among the purchasers. These brother at once rushed to the Sub-Divisional Officer and made an allegation apprehending some foul play on the part of their nephew Sanaullah Akhand. After some enquiry the Sub-Divisional Officer referred the matter to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) to whom the Certificate Officer was directly subordinate. The Additional Deputy Commissioner made a complaint in writing before the Special Judge for taking cognizance of offence of forgery against Muslim Khan, Sanaullah Akhand and others on the allegation that the accused persons by a criminal conspiracy forged the Bid-sheet and Agentnama so as to include the nama of Sanaullah Akhand by erasing the nama of Nur Mohammad Akhand. The Special Judge, however, instead of taking cognizance on the complaint by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, forwarded the matter to the Anti-Corruption Police who then investigated the case and submitted charge-sheet against the accused persons for Forgery and use of forged document by criminal conspiracy, Cognizance was taken on this police report and the accused appellants were prosecuted and tried under the provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence of 13 witnesses including a Handwriting expert and a Finger-print expert found that Abdul Ghani Akhand (PW 1), Korban Ali Akhand (PW 11) and their brother Nur Mohammad Akhand were the three auction purchasers, that this matter was correctly recorded in the Sales Register but subsequently the name of accused Sanaullah Akhand was inserted in the Bid-sheet (Exhibit 1) by erasing the nama of Nur Mohammad Akhand. The trial Court further found that accused Muslim Khan, Revenue Agent, who was admittedly engaged by the auction purchasers, had accepted an Agent-nama from them, but subsequently replaced the original Agent-nama containing the names of three brothers by a new Agent-nama (Exhibit 9) which contains the signatures of two brothers and their nephew, accused Sanaullah Akhand. The Court came to a clear finding that the Bid-sheet was forged by erasing the name of Nur Mohammad Akhand and inserting in its place the name of Sanaullah Akhand and that in the Agent-nama signature and thumb-impression, purportedly of Abdul Ghani Akhand, PW 1 and Korban Ali Akhand, PW 11, were forged and accordingly to the evidence of the two experts PWs 5 and 7, accused Sanaullah Akhand was the author of these impugned signature and finger-print. Furthermore, the Court found that the Dealing Assistant (co-accused Sayed Ahmed Patwary) acted in conspiracy with the other accused in replacing the original Agent-nama and tampering the Bid-sheet. The High Court Division on independent assessment of the evidence concurred in the findings of the trial Court. 

 4. Mr Serajul Huq, learned Advocate appeared for appellant Muslim Khan, (Revenue-Agent) and Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Advocate for appellant Sanaullah Akhand. Leave granted by us in both these appeals, filed separately, is limited to the question as to whether the cognizance was rightly taken by the Special Judge on a police report and not upon any complaint from the Court concerned, namely the Revenue Court since the Certificate Officer acted as a Revenue Court, Mr Serajul Huq has contended that the Bi sheet and the Agent-nama which were found to have been forged documents were produced in the Revenue Court in connection with a proceeding before that court and, as such, no court shall take cognizance of the offence of forgery in respect of these documents except on a complaint in writing from that court or from any other court to which that court is subordinate. Mr Huq has pointed out that a complaint was in fact filed by the higher court, namely, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), but cognizance was not taken thereupon by the Special Judge who forwarded it to the police for investigation and took cognizance on the charge sheet submitted by the police; as such, the mandatory provision of section 195 (1) (c) has been clearly violated and the trial thus held is void ab-initio. Section 195 of the Code bars the taking of cognizance except on complaint filed by certain specified public servants or Courts. It is sub-section (1) (c) of section 195 which is relevant to the instant case. It is quoted below: 

 "195 -(1) No Court shall take cognizance ...................(c) of any offence described in section 463 or punishable under section 471, section 475 or section 476 of the same Code, when such offence is alleged to have been committed by a party to any proceeding in any Court in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in such proceeding, expect on the complaint in writing of such Court, or of some other Court to which such Court is subordinate." 

 5. As I have set out at the very beginning, the first question is whether the provision of sub-section (1) (c) of section 195 of the Code has been dispensed with by the Criminal Law Amendment Act. There is no dispute that if an offence falls within the meaning of sub-section (1) (c) of section 195 Criminal Procedure Code no Court shall take cognizance of it except on a complaint from the Court concerned. But in the instant case cognizance was not taken on any complaint from Court but cognizance was taken on a police report. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division has however observed that since this case was tried under the Criminal Law Amendment Act which has prescribed a special procedure, "the provision of taking cognizance under the general law, namely section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code has been excluded" By the words "special procedure" the learned Judge has obviously meant section 4 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. This section provides that the Special Judge will take cognizance either on a complaint or on a police report. It appears that the learned Judge over looked the other provisions of this Act, particularly section 6 of the (Criminal Law Amendment) Act, 1958 This section in quoted below; 

 "Procedure in trial of cases and powers of Special Judge-(1) The provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, except those of Chapter XXXVIII of that Code, shall in so far as they are not inconsistent with this Act apply to the proceedings of the Court of a Special Judge and for the purposes of the said provisions, the Court of a Special Judge shall be deemed to be a Court of Session trying cases without aid of assessors or jury, and a person conducting prosecution before the Court of a Special Judge shall be deemed to be a Public Prosecutor." 

 This section provides that provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code shall apply to the proceedings in a case tried under the said Act in so far as they are not inconsistent with this Act. We do not find the provision of Sub-section (1) (c) section 195 of the Code requiring a complaint from Court for cognizance inconsistent with any provisions of this Act. Particularly section 4 which simply provide that the Special Judge shall have jurisdiction to take cognizance of any offence upon a complaint of facts constituting such offence or upon a report in writing by Police-officer. The learned Single Judge is of the view that when the Special Judge has got power to take cognizance on a complaint there is no necessity for the complaint to be filed by a court. But section 6 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act has specifically provided that provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code "shall apply" unless such provisions are inconsistent with the Special Act. The provision for the filing of a complaint by Court is not inconsistent with section 4 of the Act. This section provides for taking cognizance on a complaint also. But the provision for complaint from Court has not been specifically done away with, and as such, the general provision in section 195 of the Code remains unaffected. And when an offence within the meaning of sub-section (1) (c) of section 195 of the Code is committed in a proceeding before a Court then the complaint shall have to be filed by the Court or by any other court to whom that Court is subordinate. Therefore, in view of section 6 of the Act the provision as to taking cognizance on a complaint from court has remained unaffected and as such, if an offence falls within the ambit of clause (c) of section 195 (1) then cognizance cannot be taken except on a complaint from the court. 

 6. The next question is whether the facts of the instant case are such as to bring the offence committed by the appellants within the ambit of section 195 (1) (c) of the Code Mr. Serajul Huq has made strenuous efforts to bring this case within clause (c) as already quoted above. He has argued that the Bid-sheet and the Agent-nama are documents produced in connection with a proceeding in the court of the Certificate Officer and as the offence had been committed in connection with a proceeding of the Certificate Officer. It falls within this provision of section 195 (1) (c) of the Code. We are afraid; the necessary ingredients of clause (c) have not been carefully looked into by the learned Advocate. Each and every offence of forgery committed in connection with a proceeding of a Court is not covered by this clause. To bring a case within its fold, the offence must be an offence of forgery in respect of a document which is "produced or given in evidence" in that very proceeding; secondly, the offence in respect of that document must have been committed by "a party to that proceeding." These two all-important ingredients are palpably in this case. In the said proceeding, it must be kept in mind, there were two parties, the Certificate-holder, namely the Government, and the Certificate debtor, namely one Harekrishna from whom a certain amount of public money was to be recovered, but neither of them was involved in the Auction-sale in connection with which the Bid-sheet and the Agent-nama were brought into being. The documents were not produced by either of these two parties. Again, these two documents were not produced in the Certificate Proceeding itself before the Revenue Court for the Certificate Proceeding already came to an end and was disposed of before the land was put to sale. The proceeding for holding auction is a different proceeding which was not conducted by the Revenue Court, namely the Certificate Officer. It was conducted, as evidence shows, by his clerk who is co-accused Syed Ahmed Patwary. It is also necessary that after an order is passed in a Certificate Case for selling a property in auction the Certificate Officer himself will hold or conduct the sale; the sale may be conducted by any person directed by the Certificate Officer. Mr Serajul Huq argues that this sale is a continuation of the Certificate Proceeding. Even if the proceeding for sale is taken as continuation of the Certificate proceeding, still the offence committed does not come within the purview of clause (c), for these two document were not "produced or given in evidence" in the Certificate proceeding before the certificate officer because the Certificate proceeding was disposed of already. The document in respect of which an offence of forgery is committed shall have to be produced in evidence in that proceeding. The Agent-nama and the Bid-sheet are not certainly documents which were filed as evidence in that Certificate proceeding. The forged documents, it is clearly found, were neither produced it is clearly found, were neither produced as evidence in the Certificate case nor the offence in respect thereof was committed by any party to the Certificate case namely, the Certificate holder and the Certificate debtor, and as such, the offence committed by the accused appellants is not an offence within the meaning of clause (c) of section 195 (1). The provision for complaint of Court is not applicable to the trial of the appellants. We, therefore, answer the second question in the negative and find that the cognizance taken by the Special Judge is perfectly lawful.
